_readme.purpose: Working file to audit and fill in physical placement data (and any missing formulas) for every item before the engine/UI geometry revamp. One entry per item NAME, not per variant — size and geometry are identical across variants; only numeric stats differ, so those stay nested under "variants".
_readme.coordinateSystem: Plain x/y, like counting tiles on a grid: picture every item facing south (ore/effects flowing top-to-bottom), no matter which direction you would actually place it in your base — the engine handles rotating that picture to however it is really facing. (0,0) is that picture’s top-left tile, x increases right, y increases downward toward the exit. This is one fixed reference so the same number always means the same physical spot: y = 0 is the item’s own first/entrance tile, y = (length - 1) is its own last tile, y = length is the first tile immediately past its exit, y = length + 1 is one further out. A dropper’s drop point sitting "past the exit" and an upgrader’s beam sitting "on its own 2nd tile" are both just y-values on this one number line — no separate rule to remember per item type. A POINT (dropSpawn) is one {x, y} pair. A REGION (conveyor, beam, zone) is a rectangle: {x, y, width, length} — x/y is its top-left corner in this same picture, width/length is how big it is. Centering a width W on a total item width T is x = (T - W) / 2 — a whole number when that’s even, .5 when it lands on a tile seam.
_readme.howToFillBlanks: Every geometry field has a "current" value (what the engine already assumes today, with its source noted) and a "confirmed" value. Most "confirmed" values here are already PRE-FILLED with the best available assumption (furnace zones and portable beams from their real engine defaults; dropper drop points and regular-upgrader beams from reasonable guesses — centered/at-the-front for droppers, "matches the whole conveyor" for upgraders) so most of the file should already be right or close to it. Pre-filled does not mean verified — go through each one and check it in-game; if it is correct, leave it as-is (that alone is useful signal once you have actually looked); if it is wrong, overwrite "confirmed" with the real value. Each field’s "note" says whether it was a real engine default or just a reasonable guess, so you know how much scrutiny it deserves.

fields.dropSpawn: Droppers, and Ore Replicator (it also spawns a cloned ore). Where the ore visually appears, as an {x, y} point. Usually centered (x = (width-1)/2) and one tile past its own exit (y = length). Tile mapping: an integer coordinate (for example, 3) is a grid/tile boundary, so an ore centered there typically spans adjacent tiles 2 and 3; a decimal coordinate (for example, 3.4) is within its containing tile, so the ore typically stays within that tile. This is a geometry interpretation; ore size can affect overlap. Some droppers may need multiple separate points instead of one — use an array of {x, y} objects for those.
fields.conveyor: Every non-portable upgrader and furnace. The internal belt path ore rides across inside the item’s own footprint, as {x, width} — this one stays a simple pair rather than the full rectangle because a conveyor is normally assumed to run the item’s entire length (y = 0 through length). For an exceptional stepped path that does not have one constant width for the full length, use {segments: [{x, y, width, length}, ...]} to list its rectangular path segments.
fields.beam: Every upgrader, including portables. Where the item’s effect actually applies to ore, as {shape: "rect", x, y, width, length}, {shape: "radius", radius}, {shape: "sweep", axis, y, length, width, speed}, or {shape: "rotate", x, y, length, width, speed, plane?, height?, thicknessY?}. For non-portables the rect shape is currently just assumed to equal the conveyor path above — that assumption is unverified for every single item. For portables it is a separate rectangle that starts at or beyond the item’s own footprint (y >= its own length) and projects outward. "sweep" is a thin beam oscillating back and forth along one axis (used for scanners) — speed is in cycles/second (full round trips), not degrees, since nothing is actually rotating; the motion eases via sin(), fastest at the midpoint; length is the beam's fixed y-band extent (its real physical thickness, ~0.1-0.15 tiles for the 3 real sweep scanners, all look about the same so unified to 0.125 rather than guessed per-item), width is its extent along the axis it moves in. "rotate" is a straight line pivoting around a fixed point at constant angular velocity (speed in degrees/second, continuous 360°) — by default this is assumed to rotate flat in the ground plane (x,y), but set plane: "vertical" for a beam that instead rotates in the belt-width/height plane (x,z) at one fixed belt-length position (y never changes) and one fixed height above the floor (the height field) — confirmed to be how Azure Scanner actually works, not a ground-plane sweep. length for a vertical rotate is the FULL beam edge-to-edge through the pivot (a true diameter, reaching outward in both directions), not a one-sided pivot-to-tip ray. thicknessY (vertical rotate only) is the beam's real, nonzero extent along the belt's length direction — omitting it badly underestimates hit chance, see AI_DECISIONS.md 'Scanner hit-chance formulas'.
fields.zone: Furnaces only (teleporter zones are a separate conveyor-lane feature, not tracked in this item file). Where ore must physically touch to be processed for cash, as {shape: "rect", x, y, width, length}.

_readme.formulaOverride: Present on every variant of every dropper, upgrader, and furnace (null by default). Hand-added only where a plain mainStat can't express the real behavior (e.g. Wind-Up Dropper, which rolls one of several distinct value/oreSize outcomes per drop instead of having one fixed value). Not auto-generated — there is no fixed shape enforced, describe whatever the real formula actually is as clearly as possible. The "random-outcome-table" shape used for Wind-Up Dropper is {type, outcomes: [{probability, value, oreSize}], note} — reuse that shape for similar random-outcome items, or write a different shape for a genuinely different kind of formula (e.g. a size-dependent or conditional one).
_readme.variantGeometryOverrides: The top-level "geometry" block is the assumed default for every variant of an item. Some items actually change physically by variant though (e.g. a dropper that drops 1 ore at Base/Shiny but 2 ore at Mythic/Shiny Mythic) — footprint SIZE never differs across variants (verified), but things like drop points, beam reach, or zone size might. When a specific variant genuinely differs from the shared default, fill in that variant’s "geometryOverrides" object with only the field(s) that differ (same shape as the top-level "geometry" entries) instead of duplicating the whole block. Leave it null when the variant matches the default.
_readme.fileIsHandMaintained: This file is no longer auto-generated. scripts/build-item-geometry-worksheet.mjs did its one-time bootstrap and now refuses to run at all while this file exists, specifically so it can never wipe hand-typed confirmed values or fields like formulaOverride. Only direct hand edits (by the project owner or Claude, working together in conversation) should ever change this file.
_readme.conveyors: Plain conveyor belt pieces (Quarter/Half/Normal/Supercharged/Centering/Ultracharged Conveyor, Conveyor Wall, and the 4 teleporter sender/receiver pieces, which share the exact same width/length/speed shape in the engine). Unlike droppers/upgraders/furnaces, conveyors have no dropSpawn/beam/zone — ore just travels straight across them — so each entry only has size (width/length) and speed, both already real engine defaults from engine/coordinate-map.mjs's conveyorDefinitions (not guesses), kept here so they can be sanity-checked in-game the same way as everything else and have one physical place recorded. flags carries any special per-type behavior (centers, wall, teleporterColor/teleporterRole) — null when a piece has none.

variants.effects: Ores passing through Crimson Pillars are marked for up to 15 seconds, during which they may combust. If they do, the ore is destroyed and replaced by a temporary phantom zone, which provides a 1.5× multiplier to any ore that passes through it. An ore can receive this 1.5× boost a maximum of 3 times.

formulaOverride.combustionChance: Guaranteed to combust exactly once during the mark window — the moment of combustion is drawn uniformly at random from the full 15 seconds (time-to-combust ~ Uniform(0, 15s)), not an independent per-tick roll that could also result in never combusting.

spawnsPhantomZone.size: A cube whose side length in TILES equals the combusting ore's raw oreSize number directly (e.g. oreSize 1 -> a 1x1x1 tile zone) — this is NOT the ore's actual physical size. Ore physical diameter in tiles is normally oreSizeRaw / 2.5 (see AI_DECISIONS.md), so this zone comes out about 2.5x bigger per dimension than the ore that produced it.

formulaOverride.note: Requires the ore to first pass through this item's own geometry.beam (the marking zone below) — that contact is what starts the 15-second combustion window. Once marked, combustion is guaranteed (see combustionChance) and destroys the ore, replacing it with a temporary phantom zone sized per spawnsPhantomZone.size that gives every ore touching it a 1.5x multiplier, up to 3 times total per ore. The phantom zone's location is wherever the combustion happened along the ore's path (potentially many tiles past this item, or even off of it), not fixed relative to Crimson Pillars' own footprint — so unlike a normal beam/zone, it can't be expressed as geometry tied to this item.
